generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, success is tempting to read off a transcript, yet the discipline develops you in ways a grade never shows: the independence to run your own study, the care to weigh evidence, the resilience to take critical feedback. Defining success on your own terms means naming both the performance and this personal development. As you become a graduate psychologist, being able to articulate that development, with evidence from projects and placements, is what employers and training routes ask for.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students are asked, at a graduation event, what their degree gave them.

Tom answers with the classification alone: a 2:1, and relief that it is over. It is an honest account of academic performance, but it stops there. Tom has not defined success in any personal way, so there is nothing to say about who he has become, and the development that did happen goes unclaimed.

Amara answers with both kinds. The grade is there, but so is a clear account: I set out to become someone who could design a study and handle critical feedback, and here is the placement and the dissertation that show I can. That is success defined on her own terms and articulated with evidence.

Both graduated. Only Amara had defined what success meant and could articulate the development to prove it.
generatedProse.summary: Success in psychology comes in two kinds: academic performance, your results, and personal development, who you become as a psychologist. Defining success on your own terms means setting a good outcome across both, rather than inheriting a single measure. As you become a graduate, the decisive skill is articulation: saying, with evidence from your projects and placements, what you set out to do and what you can now do.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that Tom did not?

items.text: Defined success on her own terms, across both performance and personal development.
Avoided any setbacks during the degree.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara defined success on her own terms, across both kinds, and could evidence it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara could say about success, not how she scored or how fast she finished.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara defined success on her own terms across both kinds. A higher grade, greater speed or avoided setbacks are not what the example turns on.
